title: Krishna's Morning in Dvaraka
hookLine: the queens curse the roosters for crowing. Krishna gets up and keeps an ordinary morning, on purpose
carry: the ordinary morning is part of dharma
tomorrow: a sage wakes two princes in the dark. what is waiting?

cards: Dvaraka, before dawn. In the Bhagavata Purana the roosters start crowing, and Krishna's queens curse them, because the crowing means he's about to leave their side. The roosters don't care.
Krishna gets up. And then the text does something you might not expect in a story about God. It walks through his morning, step by step.
He touches water. He sits in silent meditation. He bathes, puts on clean clothes, and does his morning prayers and offerings, repeating a sacred mantra in silence, before he sees anyone at all.

teach.h: WHAT THE GREAT DO, OTHERS FOLLOW.
teach.b: Then he greets the rising sun, honors his elders, gives gifts, and only after that turns to the business of the day. Why spend all those words on God's morning?

One answer comes from Krishna himself, in the Gita: whatever the great do, others follow. If I didn't keep to my work, people everywhere would follow my lead. So the Lord keeps an ordinary morning, on purpose.

teach.h: THE MORNING IS PART OF DHARMA.
teach.b: That's the teaching: in Hindu life the ordinary morning is part of dharma, not the boring part before it. Many homes still keep its shape: a bath before worship, clean clothes, then the lamp and a prayer.
The Yoga Sutra names cleanness, shaucha, first among the observances it asks for. Ayurveda gives the same morning its own name: dinacharya.
Dina, day; charya, conduct; the day's conduct.

The Charaka Samhita's chapter on daily regimen starts with eating in the right measure, then walks through things anyone would recognize: caring for the eyes, cleaning the teeth with a twig, scraping the tongue, rinsing the mouth, oil for the body, a bath, clean clothes.
One text calls this health; the other calls it dharma. They keep the same hours. And today?
It's easy to treat the morning as something to get through before life starts. Krishna's story says the morning is where the day is first offered. The toothbrush counts.
The shower before the prayer counts.

how: Many Hindus bathe and put on clean clothes before the morning puja, then light a lamp and pray; Ayurveda's dinacharya (cleaning the teeth, scraping the tongue, oil, bath) runs alongside, and the Bhagavata's account of Krishna's morning in Dvaraka is one picture of that ordinary, sacred round.

o: a strict diet plan of what to eat at each meal
a yearly festival honoring the god of health
the day's conduct: a morning round even Krishna kept

games.q: the morning in Dvaraka — tap the pairs.
p: cursed by the queens at dawn
water, meditation, bath, clean clothes, prayer

s: in the Bhagavata, Krishna skips the ordinary morning because he is God
he bathes, dresses and prays before anything else, step by step.
in the Gita, Krishna says people follow what the great do
so he keeps to his work, as an example for everyone.
the Charaka Samhita leaves everyday things like teeth out of health
its daily-regimen chapter walks through eyes, teeth, tongue, mouth, oil, bath and clean clothes.

games.q: a friend asks why your grandmother won't start her puja until she's bathed and dressed. what's the best answer?
o: it's just habit. it doesn't mean anything.
in Hindu homes the bath is part of worship: shaucha, cleanness, comes first.
she's afraid God will be angry if she's messy.
games.why: even Krishna, in the Bhagavata, bathes and dresses before his morning prayers. the ordinary morning is part of dharma.

practice: Picture tomorrow morning, step by step: water, the sink, the shower, clean clothes. If you pray, choose one of those ordinary acts and offer it to God before you do it, the way a bath comes before puja.
If you don't pray, choose one and decide now to do it slowly and on purpose, the way the Bhagavata walks through Krishna's.

wordCard.voice: The daily routine. Dinacharya, the day's conduct: the morning round of the Ayurvedic texts, kept in Hindu homes beside the bath, the lamp and the first prayer.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dina, day, and charya, conduct. The daily round of the classical Ayurvedic texts.

carryVoice: Your line: the ordinary morning is part of dharma. Even Krishna kept one. Rest well.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.70.1–9 (the queens curse the crowing roosters; Krishna rises before dawn, touches water, meditates, bathes, dresses, performs the morning rites and silent japa, worships the rising sun, honors elders and gives gifts)
Bhagavad Gita 3.21–24 (whatever the great do, others follow; if Krishna did not act, people would follow his path)
Yoga Sutra 2.32 (the niyamas: shaucha, cleanness, first)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 5 (the chapter on measure in food and daily regimen: eye care, tooth twig, tongue scraping, mouth rinsing, oil, bathing, clean clothes)
